stem: A client receiving maintenance hemodialysis has rising serum potassium and phosphorus levels and increasing interdialytic weight gain. Which nursing action best supports appropriate interdisciplinary management?

options.A: Coordinate follow-up with the kidney dietitian so the nutrition and fluid plan can be individualized to the client's laboratory results, urine output, dialysis schedule, nutrition status, preferences, and other clinical needs.
options.B: Give the client the same fixed renal diet used for every person on hemodialysis because potassium, phosphorus, protein, and fluid goals do not need individual adjustment.
options.C: Delay dietitian involvement until severe malnutrition develops because routine nutrition assessment is outside the dialysis plan of care.
options.D: Tell the client to eliminate all potassium- and phosphorus-containing foods without reviewing laboratory values, overall nutrition, or the prescribed dialysis plan.

rationale: Current National Kidney Foundation guidance emphasizes that there is no single kidney diet that is appropriate for every client. For people on hemodialysis, the kidney dietitian develops an individualized plan using factors such as laboratory results, residual urine output, dialysis schedule, nutrition status, weight trends, culture, budget, food preferences, and other health conditions. Dialysis nutrition commonly requires attention to protein, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and fluid, but the degree of restriction varies by the individual. Therefore, A is correct. B and D use nonindividualized blanket restrictions, and C delays an established component of interdisciplinary dialysis care.
educational_objective: Coordinate individualized renal nutrition care for a client on hemodialysis by involving the kidney dietitian and using current laboratory, dialysis, residual-kidney-function, and nutrition data rather than applying a universal renal diet.
source_organization: National Kidney Foundation; Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
source_document_title: Hemodialysis and Your Diet; Creating a Kidney Friendly Plate; End-Stage Renal Disease Facilities — Conditions for Coverage
source_version_date: NKF hemodialysis diet guidance last updated 2024-08-28; NKF kidney-friendly plate updated 2026-06-05; CMS ESRD CfC resource current in 2026
source_locator: NKF 'Hemodialysis and Your Diet' → kidney dietitian develops the diet using laboratory results, urine output, hemodialysis schedule, and nutrition status; sections on protein, sodium, potassium, phosphorus and fluid emphasize individualized needs. NKF 'Creating a Kidney Friendly Plate' → no single kidney diet works for everyone; plan varies by CKD stage, labs, dialysis/transplant status, appetite, weight, medicines, budget, culture and preferences. CMS ESRD Conditions for Coverage → dialysis facilities must meet patient-centered clinical and interdisciplinary care requirements.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports individualized dietitian-led nutrition planning for hemodialysis clients based on current clinical data rather than a universal fixed renal diet.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care → Collaboration/Referrals/Continuity of Care: coordinate interprofessional services, make appropriate referrals, and integrate individualized client data and preferences into the plan of care.
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — interdisciplinary renal nutrition coordination during hemodialysis
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's specialty-role recall item into an applied Management-of-Care decision. The final item preserves the renal dietitian construct but emphasizes individualized nutrition planning based on current labs, residual urine output, dialysis schedule and nutrition status, avoiding the false implication that every CKD/ESRD client receives identical protein, sodium, potassium, phosphorus and fluid restrictions.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Interdisciplinary renal nutrition management during hemodialysis
audit_findings.source_authority: Current National Kidney Foundation dialysis nutrition guidance with CMS ESRD facility standards used for interdisciplinary-care context.
audit_findings.currentness: NKF has current 2026 nutrition guidance explicitly stating that kidney diets must be individualized; the hemodialysis-specific page remains current and medically reviewed.

claim_by_claim.stem: Rising potassium/phosphorus and interdialytic weight gain are clinically coherent findings that justify reassessment of nutrition/fluid management without presuming one cause.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because NKF explicitly describes individualized kidney-dietitian planning using labs, urine output, treatment schedule and nutrition status.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because current NKF guidance states there is no single kidney diet suitable for everyone and needs vary across patients and treatment modalities.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because nutrition assessment and dietitian involvement are routine components of dialysis care, not interventions reserved for severe malnutrition.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because blanket elimination can create nutritional harm and ignores the individualized laboratory and treatment context.
claim_by_claim.rationale: Avoids unsupported universal nutrient limits or fluid volumes and does not assign medical prescribing authority to the RN.
claim_by_claim.educational_objective: Specific to referral and coordination of individualized renal nutrition care.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B tests one-size-fits-all diet thinking, C delayed interdisciplinary referral, and D indiscriminate restriction. Each is realistic and distinct.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A integrates current client data and the appropriate interdisciplinary specialist without imposing unsupported blanket restrictions.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are complete nursing management approaches to the same dialysis nutrition problem and use comparable structure.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care is the strongest fit because the central task is interprofessional coordination and individualized care planning.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited whether the item should instead test Basic Care and Comfort nutrition. Because the stem asks what the RN should do to coordinate a specialized individualized plan, the primary physician task is care coordination/referral rather than direct food selection. No unresolved conflict remains.
